title: Amos 4:1–5
context: Amos, a herdsman of Tekoa sent to the northern kingdom in the days of Jeroboam the son of Joash (Amos 1:1), turns to the wealthy of Samaria. He calls them “cows of Bashan,” a region known for rich pasture, and the Lord GOD swears an oath of exile against them. Then the LORD speaks in bitter irony, inviting Israel to keep crowding the shrines at Bethel and Gilgal. Shared ground: both traditions read this as judgment on worship that sits comfortably beside oppression of the poor.

verses.text: Listen to this word, you cows of Bashan, who are on the mountain of Samaria, who oppress the poor, who crush the needy, who tell their husbands, “Bring us drinks!”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the charge is concrete: the women of Samaria “oppress the poor” and “crush the needy” by demanding luxury from their husbands. Responsibility is personal and shared within the household, and the prophet addresses them directly as people able to hear and answer.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise stress that the indictment is specific and just. The image of fattened cows on Samaria’s hill exposes a comfort built on others’ suffering. Shared ground: God sees the private demands that drive public injustice, and he holds the comfortable to account.

verses.text: The Lord GOD has sworn by his holiness, “Behold, the days shall come on you that they will take you away with hooks, and the last of you with fish hooks.
verses.arminianNotes: The Lord GOD “has sworn by his holiness,” binding the threat to his own character. Arminian readers see holiness as the reason sin cannot be ignored; the oath shows the seriousness of a judgment that the people’s long refusal has brought near.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the oath as God pledging his own holy nature that the sentence will stand. The hooks picture captives led away like animals. Shared ground: God’s holiness is not only purity but active opposition to oppression, and his word does not fail.

verses.text: You will go out at the breaks in the wall, everyone straight before her; and you will cast yourselves into Harmon,” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: The women will leave through breaches in the wall, each straight ahead, a picture of a city already broken. “Harmon” is uncertain; interpreters offer several suggestions, and none is settled. Arminian readers keep the focus on the certainty of exile rather than the place name.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also leave the location open and note the closing formula, “says the LORD”, which seals the oracle. Shared ground: the people who once lounged on Samaria’s mountain will be driven out through its broken walls, and the word comes from the LORD himself.

verses.text: “Go to Bethel, and sin; to Gilgal, and sin more. Bring your sacrifices every morning, your tithes every three days,
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD speaks in irony: “Go to Bethel, and sin”. Arminian readers hear a rebuke of religious zeal that changes nothing in the heart. Frequent sacrifices and tithes are not condemned in themselves, but they cannot cover lives that crush the needy.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hear the same sarcasm and see worship turned into self-display. Bethel and Gilgal had sacred memories, yet they became places to sin more. Shared ground: outward devotion without justice and faithfulness only adds to guilt before God.

verses.text: offer a sacrifice of thanksgiving of that which is leavened, and proclaim free will offerings and brag about them; for this pleases you, you children of Israel,” says the Lord GOD.
verses.arminianNotes: The worshipers “brag about” their offerings, and the LORD names the motive: “this pleases you”. Arminian readers see worship that has become self-pleasing rather than God-pleasing, a warning that religious activity can be chosen as a substitute for obedience.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress the same diagnosis: the people worship to satisfy themselves. Shared ground: God weighs the heart behind the offering, and worship centered on human approval is rejected, whatever its frequency or generosity.
